prompt.context: Your client is a national drug-store that is adding a new type of hair dye to its retail offering. 'Highlights Dye' allows customers to comb in small amounts of various color to hair rather than the traditional method of dying the whole head. The client is considering launching its own in-house brand or carrying an existing recognized brand-name called 'Vibrants'. The retail chain already carries their in-house brand across many products (toothpaste, cotton swabs, etc.), including traditional hair dye in both temporary and permanent varieties. 'Highlights Dye' is a fashion-forward product available in natural and florescent colors; each application lasts roughly 30 days. The target customer is under 30 years of age. The business objective is profitability and the timeline is 90 days to launch.
prompt.question: Should the drugstore carry Vibrants over the in-store brand?

clarifying_info.q: Does the store already have an in-house brand in this category?
clarifying_info.a: No, but it carries in-house brands in many other categories including traditional hair dye

clarifying_info.q: Can the store change the retail price of Vibrants or run promotions?
clarifying_info.a: No — if carrying Vibrants, the drugstore is unable to change the retail price or run price promotions

exhibits.title: Pricing Considerations
exhibits.shows: A table comparing retail and wholesale prices per 1,000 units for the In-House Brand and Vibrants, plus a note on the anticipated market size

data.Note: Prices are per 1,000 units; if selling Vibrants the drugstore cannot change retail price or run price promotions

exhibits.title: Sample Focus Group Answers
exhibits.shows: A table of focus group respondents with columns for Gender, Age, and Answer (Y/N) to the question: 'Would you purchase a store-brand version of Vibrants over the brand name?'

framework: Product attributes specific to Highlights Dye: application length (temporary ~30 days), color varieties (natural vs. florescent), application process (home vs. salon), ingredients (chemical vs. natural dye)
Cost and margin analysis: compare unit economics of in-house brand vs. Vibrants at both retail and wholesale prices
Market and competitor context: size of addressable market, existing competitors, market trends (fashion-forward hair color)
Target customer segmentation: fashion-conscious youth, natural/aging customers covering grey hair, DIYers avoiding salon prices
Capabilities and launch feasibility: R&D, manufacturing, packaging, and promotion costs to develop in-house brand vs. 90-day launch window
Opportunity costs and cannibalization: effect on existing in-house hair dye products

questions.prompt: Calculate and compare the profit margin per unit for the In-House Brand vs. Vibrants
questions.guidance: Candidate should read the footnote that prices are per 1,000 units to simplify arithmetic. Margin = Retail price minus Wholesale cost. The in-house brand has a higher absolute and percentage margin, making it financially superior on a per-unit basis.

math.setup: Margin per 1,000 units = Retail price − Wholesale cost. Margin % = Margin / Retail price.
steps: In-house brand margin (60%) is approximately double Vibrants margin (31%)
math.answer: In-House Brand margin: $3,000 per 1,000 units (60%); Vibrants margin: $2,000 per 1,000 units (~31%). In-house brand has superior margins.

questions.prompt: Analyze the focus group data. What does it tell you about customer preferences by age group?
questions.guidance: Candidate must note the question is phrased inversely — 'Yes' means willingness to buy the store-brand INSTEAD of Vibrants. The target customer is under 30. A strong candidate separates the data by age bracket: under-30 respondents overwhelmingly prefer Vibrants (only 1 of 8 said Yes to store-brand = 12.5%); over-30 respondents all prefer the store-brand (3 of 3 said Yes = 100%). Key insight: the target customer (under 30) strongly prefers the Vibrants brand name over the in-house alternative. A strong candidate may also question sample size and can be told it accurately represents a larger study.

math.setup: Separate respondents by age <30 and ≥30; count Yes vs. No for each group
steps: Under 30 respondents: F/29/N, F/27/N, F/24/Y, M/25/N, F/29/N, F/26/N, F/23/N, F/28/N → 8 respondents, 1 Yes (F/24)
Over 30 respondents: M/33/Y, M/31/Y, M/31/Y → 3 respondents, 3 Yes
math.answer: Under-30 (target customer): only 12.5% would buy the store-brand over Vibrants. Over-30: 100% would buy the store-brand. The target customer strongly prefers Vibrants.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the client consider when deciding whether to develop an in-house brand vs. adopt Vibrants within the 90-day timeline?

categories.name: In-house brand development requirements
ideas: R&D to formulate highlight dye in multiple colors
Manufacturing setup or contract manufacturer sourcing

categories.name: Timeline risk
ideas: 90-day window is very tight for new product development
Vibrants is already developed, tested, and branded
In-house development risk of missing launch window
Competitive disadvantage if shelf is empty while trend is hot

categories.name: Financial trade-offs
ideas: In-house margin is 60% vs. ~31% for Vibrants
Start-up costs for in-house brand may offset margin advantage
No pricing flexibility with Vibrants brand
In-house brand could cannibalize existing traditional hair dye lines

categories.name: Customer and brand considerations
ideas: Target customer (under 30) strongly prefers Vibrants brand name
Brand recognition and trust already established with Vibrants
Risk of store-brand perception as lower quality among fashion-conscious youth
Long-term: if in-house brand succeeds, higher margin and full pricing control

recommendation: The drugstore should carry Vibrants rather than launching its own in-house brand

Despite the in-house brand having superior margins (60% vs. ~31%), the target customer segment (under 30) is overwhelmingly unwilling to purchase the store-brand alternative — only 12.5% would choose it over Vibrants
The 90-day launch timeline makes in-house brand development infeasible given required R&D, manufacturing, packaging, and promotional investments
risks: Fashion-forward demand for highlight dye may be a trend that fades, reducing long-term viability
Carrying Vibrants means no pricing flexibility and no ability to run promotions, limiting competitive response
Lower margins per unit compared to in-house brand could reduce overall profitability if market grows
next_steps: Develop a marketing plan targeting under-30 customers and allocate appropriate shelf space
Procure initial Vibrants orders aligned to the $750,000 anticipated market
Monitor trend durability; if demand proves sustained, revisit in-house brand development to capture higher margins longer term
